overview: Communities associated with Chief Roi Mata in central Vanuatu maintain traditions linking chiefly authority, social responsibilities and particular places. The last chief's death did not end this living cultural landscape.

items.text: Sites on Efate, Lelepa and Artok commemorate the last Roi Mata's residence, death and burial in the early seventeenth century. This period is not a precise founding date.
Chiefs derive authority through earlier title holders. Roi Mata's social reforms and approaches to resolving disputes remain a source of guidance.
Tabu restrictions on the residence and burial places have shaped land use for centuries. Spiritual responsibilities therefore influence the physical landscape.
Oral traditions and archaeological evidence contribute complementary records of Roi Mata's world. Community memory remains central to understanding the sites.
Local communities and government bodies share heritage management, alongside chiefly authority and customary prohibitions. Preservation draws on living institutions.
